title: Short Division Strip
description: Do the steps of long division in your head, write each leftover small beside the next digit, and still write every zero.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit.

writeup.why: Divide by one digit in your head, writing only the answer and the small leftovers, and find out that nothing of the long method has gone missing.
writeup.look: One strip across the stage with the divisor behind a bar, the quotient row under it, and the long lane below that.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Short Division Strip' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the quotient digits written against the digits of the dividend, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each digit settles under the strip, a zero counted like any other, and the second fixed at how many cells the strip has. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The times table card stands at the left of the working area, 120 by 480 at 64,220, reading the divisor times one to times nine in rose; it is read and never tapped for an answer. A tag row runs across the top, 600 by 40 at 350,212, and names the number being divided at the cell in hand with its place name, thirty-six ones and never a bare thirty-six. The strip runs under it, 840 by 110 at 210,260: the divisor in amber in a cell 120 wide at its left behind a short upright bar, then the dividend's digits in deep blue in cells 150 wide, each under its place heading from thousands to ones. The quotient row lies directly under the strip, 600 by 90 at 350,374, one empty cell under each digit, and each quotient digit settles in green in the cell under the digit it came from. What is left at a step is written small and raised, in vermilion, at the upper left of the next digit's cell, and the small numeral and that digit then light together as one number while the tag row names it. The zero guard is a hinged cover over the quotient cell in hand. It takes a zero only when the number made by the small leftover and the digit is smaller than the divisor, and writes it in grey at full size; a zero offered anywhere else is handed back with the facts on the times table card that fit lit, at least the first of them, and the child's offer written beside the cell. The long lane runs under the quotient row, 840 by 270 at 210,456, and writes the same division in full, one row per step: the working number with its place name, the multiple taken away in rose, and what is left in vermilion. Each quotient digit lights in both lanes at once when the two agree, a digit that disagrees lights only where it was written with the step that made it lit in the long lane, and the final remainders of the two lanes are drawn level at the right hand end. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a quotient digit or a leftover is asked for, and a small key beside them writes a leftover raised beside the next digit instead of in the quotient row, so the two can never be mixed. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The small leftover is small in size only. It is drawn at full strength, never faded or ghosted, and it stays beside its digit after the step is done, because in short division it is the whole of the written working.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last strip the child worked, every small leftover still beside its digit, with the long lane under it agreeing digit for digit.

phases.win: the quotient row fills and the long lane below shows the same digits it would have written
phases.does: divides each digit in turn and writes only the quotient digit under it
phases.goal: short division does the steps of long division in the head and writes only the quotient
phases.says: Divide the tens, then the ones. Write only the answer.
phases.check: Away from the screen: divide sixty-three by three in your head, saying each step with its place name. Write only the answer.
phases.feels: nothing of the long way has gone, it has only stopped being written down
phases.hands: Put eight tens and six ones in play money on the table with two envelopes. Share them without writing anything down, saying each step aloud with its place name. Then write only the answer, and let a partner write the long way underneath from what they heard.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: which digit did you divide first? Second rung, the phase's: what place is it in? Third rung: the long lane opens with its first step already written, and the child copies only the quotient digit up into the strip. The number pad stays open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: it looks nothing like the long way on the page, and with no working written there is nothing to compare it with.
wrong.move: thinks the short way is a separate trick that could give a different answer from the long way.
wrong.screen: the long lane is worked from the same digits while the child fills the strip, and each quotient digit it writes lights the matching cell above at the same moment: eight tens by four is two tens in both lanes, and four ones by four is one in both. The two rows of digits are drawn level, with nothing marked.

wrong.why: with nothing written down the middle digit is the easiest one to lose, and a zero seems to fill the gap it leaves.
wrong.move: writes two hundred and two for eight hundred and forty-eight divided by four, working the hundreds and the ones and losing the tens in the middle.
wrong.screen: the guard over the tens cell hands the zero back, because four tens is not smaller than four, and the long lane works that step in full beneath it: four tens by four, one ten. The strip's tens cell takes the one, and the child's two hundred and two stays written beside the row.

phases.screen: a two-digit dividend on the strip with the divisor behind its bar and the quotient row empty
phases.soWhat: Short division does the steps of long division in the head and writes only the quotient.
phases.concept: The same steps, kept in your head

phases.win: the small leftover and the digit light together as one number and the next quotient digit lands
phases.does: writes the leftover small beside the next digit and divides the number the two make
phases.goal: each leftover is written small beside the next digit and joins it
phases.says: Something is left. Where does it go? What number does it make?
phases.check: Divide ninety-one by seven the short way. Say what the small number beside the one stands for.
phases.feels: the leftover tens have not gone anywhere, they have been changed into ones and put beside the ones already there
phases.hands: Share seven tens and two ones among three envelopes in play money. When one ten will not go round, change it for ten ones and put them beside the two ones already on the table. Count the ones now there, and share them. Then write the division the short way, with the changed ten written small beside the two.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what was left after the step before? Second rung, the phase's: where is it written, and what number does it make with the next digit? Third rung: the strip is cut to two digits with one carry, and the long lane writes the carry out in full above it. The number pad and the small key stay open.

wrong.why: the small three is the smallest mark on the strip, and the digit printed in the cell looks like the whole of the next number.
wrong.move: divides the six on its own and drops the three that was carried.
wrong.screen: the child's step is run in the long lane as six ones by seven, which gives nothing, while the three tens left from the step before stay lit in that lane, still waiting. The check under the lanes rebuilds the child's answer as five hundred and sixty-six, thirty short of the dividend. The small three is then walked into place beside the six, the two light together as thirty-six ones, and the step runs again.

wrong.why: a small number beside a digit looks like something to add, and in every sum met before this chapter that is exactly what it was.
wrong.move: adds the carried three to the six and divides nine, as a carried number was used in adding.
wrong.screen: the long lane changes the three tens into thirty ones and lays them beside the six ones, and the tag row reads thirty-six ones, not nine. The child's nine stays written above the tag, and the check under the lanes rebuilds the child's answer, eighty-one remainder two, as five hundred and sixty-nine, twenty-seven short of the dividend.

phases.screen: a three-digit dividend where the first step leaves something over
phases.soWhat: Each leftover is written small beside the next digit and joins it.
phases.concept: Carry the leftover to the next digit

phases.win: the zero settles under its digit and the digit slides on to join the next one
phases.does: compares each number with the divisor, writes the zero where it is smaller, and carries the whole digit on
phases.goal: a zero goes in the quotient whenever the number is smaller than the divisor, and only then
phases.says: Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then what goes underneath?
phases.check: Divide five thousand four hundred and fifteen by five the short way. Which digit gets a zero underneath, and why?
phases.feels: a step with something left over can still fit the divisor, and the only step that gets a zero is one where the divisor fits no times at all
phases.hands: Write three short divisions on the board with their strips blank. In each, have the class say, digit by digit, the number being divided with its place name and whether it is smaller than the divisor, before any digit is written underneath. Write a zero only where they say smaller. Then ask which steps left something over and still got a digit.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what number is being divided under this cell, with the small leftover joined on? Second rung, the phase's: is it smaller than the divisor? Third rung: the times table card lights its first fact only, and the child says whether even that one fits. The zero key stays open, and the guard still reads it.

wrong.why: the summary box two topics back ties a zero to a digit that is not divisible, and in short division no written step shows that the divisor fitted. The test that decides it is smaller than the divisor, and nothing on the page asks for it.
wrong.move: writes a zero under every digit whose step leaves a remainder, because it does not divide exactly.
wrong.screen: the guard hands back each zero offered at a step that is not smaller than the divisor, and lights on the times table card the facts that fit: twenty-seven tens takes four sixes and thirty-five ones takes five. Only under the two hundreds, where two is smaller than six, does the guard open and take the grey zero. The child's zeros stay written beside their cells, and the long lane works each step in full underneath.

wrong.why: in short division the zero step leaves nothing to write but the zero itself, so the step can pass in the head without a mark.
wrong.move: writes sixty-three for four thousand eight hundred and twenty-four divided by eight, leaving out the zero where two tens are smaller than eight.
wrong.screen: the tens cell of the quotient row is lit empty between the six and the three. The guard opens over it, because two tens is smaller than eight, and takes the grey zero, and the two tens are carried small beside the four. The check under the lanes rebuilds the child's sixty-three as five hundred and four, beside the four thousand eight hundred and twenty-four.

phases.screen: a dividend with one digit smaller than the divisor and another step that leaves a remainder
phases.soWhat: A zero goes in the quotient whenever the number is smaller than the divisor, and only then.
phases.concept: A zero still has to be written

phases.win: each quotient digit lights in both lanes together and the two remainders stand level
phases.does: works the short strip, then the long lane, and compares the two answers digit by digit
phases.goal: long and short division give the same quotient and remainder
phases.says: Do it both ways. Do the answers match?
phases.check: Divide eight hundred and nineteen by four both ways. Show where the short way's small number appears in the long way.
phases.feels: two ways of writing the same steps, and a disagreement points to one step rather than a vote between two answers
phases.hands: Pairs take one card. One partner divides the long way on paper and the other the short way, and they race. When both have finished, they lay the two sheets side by side and match the quotients digit by digit, and the short way's small numbers against the long way's leftovers. Where they differ, they find the first step that differs.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: do the first digits of both lanes match? Second rung, the phase's: at which step do the lanes first part? Third rung: both lanes are cut to a two-digit dividend with one carry, and the child works them side by side. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the long way looks more careful and the short way looks quicker, and either one can feel like the one to believe.
wrong.move: trusts one way over the other when the two disagree, instead of looking for the step that slipped.
wrong.screen: the two lanes are compared cell by cell from the left, each matching digit lighting in both, and the first cell that does not match stops the comparison and lights the step behind it in the long lane. Both answers stay written, and that one step is worked again in both lanes at once.

wrong.why: seven tens smaller than nine gives nothing to say in the head, and the seven slides on to join the eight without the zero being written.
wrong.move: gives sixty-eight remainder six for five thousand four hundred and seventy-eight divided by nine, the short way losing the zero the long way writes.
wrong.screen: the long lane writes the step in full, seven tens by nine, no nines, and puts a grey zero in the tens place, and the strip's tens cell lights empty against it. The check under the lanes rebuilds the child's answer as six hundred and eighteen, beside the five thousand four hundred and seventy-eight.

phases.screen: one division loaded in the short strip and in the long lane, both unworked
phases.soWhat: Long and short division give the same quotient and remainder.
phases.concept: Long or short, the same answer

writeup.delight: The fourth phase, when the long lane is worked under a finished strip. Each quotient digit the long lane writes travels up and lights the same digit in the strip's quotient row, and each leftover the long lane writes in full slides up and settles onto the small raised numeral the strip already carries, fitting it exactly. The two remainders arrive at the right hand end on the same tick and stand level. It can be run as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a two-digit dividend stands in the strip with the divisor behind its bar, the quotient row empty and the long lane drawn empty beneath it. On the second a three-digit dividend stands with its first quotient digit already written and the space beside the next digit empty, waiting for what was left. On the third a dividend stands with one digit smaller than the divisor, the guard closed over the quotient cell under that digit, and a later step that will leave something over. On the fourth one division is loaded in the strip and in the long lane together, both unworked. The running count at the top left holds the quotient digits written against the digits of the dividend, and the answer slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first digit cell, or the empty space beside the next digit, or the guard, or the long lane's first row, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which digit comes first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any dividend up to four digits and any divisor from two to nine, with the long lane and the times table card open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on short division by one digit, carrying each leftover, writing every zero, and checking the short way against the long way.
voiceLines: One strip, a divisor behind its bar, and the working kept in your head. Which digit first?
Divide the tens, then the ones. Write only the answer.
Something is left. Where does it go? What number does it make?
Is this number smaller than the divisor? Then what goes underneath?
Do it both ways. Do the answers match?
A new strip. Say the divisor's times table before the first digit.
Free play. Any dividend, any divisor from two to nine, with the long lane and the table card open.
Say the step out loud with its place name, and look at the long lane under it.
Every leftover carried small, every zero written where the number was smaller, and both lanes agreeing.

observations.why: Short division does the same steps as long division and only leaves the working unwritten.
observations.soWhat: Short division is long division done in the head, so it cannot give a different answer.
observations.observe: The quotient row filled while the long lane underneath wrote out every step the strip had kept in the head.

observations.why: What is left of the tens is still tens, and changed into ones it joins the ones already there.
observations.soWhat: Each leftover is written small beside the next digit and is divided together with it.
observations.observe: The small leftover and the next digit lit together and were read as one number.

observations.why: A zero means the divisor does not fit at all, and that happens only when the number is smaller than the divisor.
observations.soWhat: A zero goes in the quotient when the number is smaller than the divisor. A step that is not divisible but not smaller still gets a digit.
observations.observe: The guard took a zero under one digit and handed one back under another digit whose step left something over.

observations.why: The two ways make the same steps in the same order, so a difference can only come from one step.
observations.soWhat: Long and short division always give the same quotient and remainder, and checking one against the other finds a slip exactly.
observations.observe: When the two lanes disagreed, only the step that slipped was lit in the long lane.

phases.screen: a two-digit dividend on the strip with the divisor behind its bar and the quotient row empty
phases.win: the quotient row fills and the long lane below shows the same digits it would have written
phases.traceback: The check rebuilds the child's answer, then the long lane works each step with its place name and each quotient digit it writes lights the same cell in the strip, ending on the whole quotient.
ladder: Which digit did you divide first? Short division starts with the biggest place.
Which quotient digit belongs under the tens, and which under the ones?
Did the tens get a quotient digit of their own?

phases.screen: a three-digit dividend where the first step leaves something over
phases.win: the small leftover and the digit light together as one number and the next quotient digit lands
phases.traceback: The check rebuilds the child's answer beside the dividend; then each leftover is written small beside the next digit, the two light together as one number while the tag names it, and the long lane writes the step in full, ending on the quotient and remainder.
ladder: What was left after the tens step, and where did it go?
What was left after dividing the tens, and which digit does it sit beside?
Each step leaves something. Did you join it to the next digit every time?
Where is it written, and what number does it make with the next digit?
The long lane changes the leftover into the next place. Read the number it makes there.

phases.screen: a dividend with one digit smaller than the divisor and another step that leaves a remainder
phases.win: the zero settles under its digit and the digit slides on to join the next one
phases.traceback: The check rebuilds the child's answer; then each step is weighed against the divisor with its fitting fact lit on the table card, a grey zero goes in only where the number is smaller (the long lane says no sixes), and the strip ends on the whole quotient and remainder.
ladder: A step with something left over can still fit the divisor. Which numbers were really smaller than it?
After the hundreds step, what number stands in the tens, and does eight fit into it?
Every place gets a digit. What goes under a number smaller than the divisor?
Is it smaller than the divisor?
Try the divisor times one. If even that does not fit, a zero goes underneath.

phases.screen: one division loaded in the short strip and in the long lane, both unworked
phases.win: each quotient digit lights in both lanes together and the two remainders stand level
phases.traceback: The check rebuilds the child's answer beside the dividend; then both lanes are worked step by step, each quotient digit lighting in the strip and the long lane together, and the two remainders end level.
ladder: Do the first digits of both lanes match? Then look at the next step.
Which step of the long way did Meena's short way skip?
Did the short way carry what was left after the hundreds into the tens?
At which step do the two lanes first part?
Work that one step again in both lanes, and say it with its place name.

lanes: the short strip: divisor behind its bar, dividend under place headings, quotient row, remainder
the long lane: one row per step (number in hand with its place name, quotient digit, multiple taken away, what is left)
the check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The check rebuilds the child's answer, then the long lane works each step with its place name and each quotient digit it writes lights the same cell in the strip, ending on the whole quotient.

Phase 2: The check rebuilds the child's answer beside the dividend; then each leftover is written small beside the next digit, the two light together as one number while the tag names it, and the long lane writes the step in full, ending on the quotient and remainder.

Phase 3: The check rebuilds the child's answer; then each step is weighed against the divisor with its fitting fact lit on the table card, a grey zero goes in only where the number is smaller (the long lane says no sixes), and the strip ends on the whole quotient and remainder.

Phase 4: The check rebuilds the child's answer beside the dividend; then both lanes are worked step by step, each quotient digit lighting in the strip and the long lane together, and the two remainders end level.

voice.opening: One strip, a divisor behind its bar, and the working kept in your head. Which digit first?
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs
voice.onFinish: Every leftover carried small, every zero written where the number was smaller, and both lanes agreeing.
voice.rules: Spoken on opening, as each phase begins, on each question, on a miss and on the summary page. Every line is printed in the bubble, numbers as words, by the device's own voice (Indian English first). Muting keeps the child's place; unmuting speaks on from the word it reached. If the browser refuses speech until a tap, the first line waits behind a Tap to start cover.

guide.playsOn: none: an Udgam tool opens straight on its phase; the phase's teach lines are spoken first, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

items.planQuestion: A child works 6275 divided by 6 by short division and writes a zero at every step that leaves something over. Which zero is right, and what is the quotient?

question.en: Ravi works 6,275 divided by 6. He writes a zero at every step that leaves something over. Which zero is right? Find the real quotient and remainder.

items.planAnswer: Only the zero in the hundreds is right, because 2 hundreds is smaller than 6. The quotient is 1045, remainder 5

items.planAnswer: It should be 608 remainder 6. The long way shows that 7 tens is smaller than 9, so a zero goes in the tens of the quotient; 9 times 608 is 5472, add 6 makes 5478

items.planAnswer: 791 both ways. The short way carries 3 into the hundreds, making 31, and 3 into the tens, making 36
